question: What changes when a moving dance acquires a fixed bass note?
intro: A G-major minuet frames a musette, whose sustained bass recalls the drone of a bagpipe. This selection combines different pianists and omits the fourth movement, the Rigaudon; it is not a complete performance of the suite.

sections.label: Menuet · repeated strains
sections.mNote: The G-major dance balances melody against a moving bass.

sections.label: Musette · sustained bass
sections.mNote: A drone supports a more chordal, modal dance.

sections.label: Menuet · changed accompaniment
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns above material from the musette.

sections.label: Closing expansion
sections.mNote: A final swell yields to spacious, slowing gestures.

cues.title: Three beats, one phrase
cues.text: The minuet moves in three, but the melody extends across the bar lines. Listen to the bass as well as the tune: it helps the dance move forward without making every first beat a heavy accent.
cues.evidence: Durand 1918 piano score, printed p. 20: Allegro moderato, 3/4, G major, long slurs and independent bass motion. This describes the opening rather than claiming a particular accent in the recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Remembering Jean Dreyfus
cues.text: The Menuet is dedicated to Jean Dreyfus, killed in the First World War. His stepmother, Madame Fernand Dreyfus, corresponded with Ravel during the war and received him at her Normandy home during his recovery. The memorial is also tied to a household that supported him.
cues.evidence: Dedication in Durand score, p. 20, and BnF https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Family relationship, correspondence and Normandy stay: Kansas City Symphony programme, printed pp. 5–6, https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf.

cues.title: Dance as a remembered form
cues.text: The minuet is an inherited courtly dance, not a reconstruction of one particular eighteenth-century piece. Ravel uses its balanced phrases and triple metre while allowing the harmony to stray beyond the simple chord patterns suggested by the movement’s old-fashioned title.
cues.evidence: Orchestre national de Lyon programme discusses Ravel’s homage to French eighteenth-century music and the Menuet’s form: https://www.auditorium-lyon.com/en/node/13646. The Durand score supplies the 3/4 metre, repeated strains and chromatic harmony; no quotation of a specific older minuet is claimed.

cues.title: A bass that stays
cues.text: The central musette recalls a bagpipe through its sustained bass. Above that drone, the chords can move while the foundation stays put. Listen for the difference between a bass that guides the harmony by changing notes and one that makes the changing harmony rub against it.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 21, heading “Musette” and sustained bass notes. Analysis candidates at 110 and 114 seconds accompany a fall in attack density to roughly 1.4–1.8 per second. The point is an approximate passage location, not a measured bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The musette grows
cues.text: The drone does not mean the music must remain small. The central passage swells markedly before subsiding. Follow the upper chords as they gain weight against that comparatively stable bass foundation.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 21, musette crescendo to ff and subsequent reduction. Analysis rises from −18.3 dB at 140 seconds to −11.2 at 145 and −8.7 at 155, then falls to −18.7 at 165.

cues.title: Two ideas heard together
cues.text: The returning minuet is not a literal reset. Ravel brings back the opening melody above an accompaniment that retains the musette’s chordal character. Listen for recognition in the tune and change underneath it: the middle section has altered how the opening can return.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 22, opening melody with musette-derived accompaniment; Lyon programme describes the ABA design. Analysis boundary candidate at 188 seconds helps locate the return approximately. The cue anticipates the passage and does not claim the first returning note at 180.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A later orchestral life
cues.text: The Menuet was one of the four movements Ravel orchestrated in 1919. This is the original piano version: the changing colours have to come from touch, register and the balance between voices, not from replacing one orchestral instrument with another.
cues.evidence: The original piano version is identified by BnF and the selected Commons file. The 1919 orchestral selection is documented in the Lyon programme: https://www.auditorium-lyon.com/en/node/13646.

cues.title: A final dynamic crest
cues.text: The late swell reaches the performance’s strongest measured level before dropping sharply. Listen beyond that crest: Ravel still has a quieter ending to make, so this expansion is not the last word.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ravel-tombeau-menuet.txt: the 250-second window is the loudest at −8.3 dB; 255 falls to −18.0 and 260 to −23.7. Durand score, p. 23, has a late expansion followed by quiet closing material.

cues.title: Time allowed to settle
cues.text: The final page asks for considerable slowing and then a very slow close. The wider spaces between gestures let the piano’s resonance become part of the phrase. Hear the ending as a deliberate release of the dance’s pulse, not merely a quieter repeat.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 23: “Ralentir beaucoup” and “Très lent”. Analysis shows sparse attacks and a decay from −19.2 dB at 285 seconds to −48.6 at 295; the cue identifies the closing passage, not a computed tempo curve.

transitions.title: Moving bass becomes drone
transitions.how: The minuet’s repeated strains give way to a musette. Instead of continuing the earlier mobile bass, Ravel sustains a drone under chordal upper parts. Triple metre remains, so the change of character comes from the bass, the modal colour and the spacing of attacks rather than a new metre.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 20–21, transition into the labelled Musette and sustained bass. Analysis candidates at 110 and 114 seconds with fewer attacks support the approximate location; no exact bar boundary is asserted.

transitions.title: The tune brings something back
transitions.how: The opening G-major melody returns, but the musette’s accompaniment remains beneath it. Ravel joins the two sections by combination: the tune supplies recognition while the lower parts retain a memory of the middle. The return therefore changes the opening’s texture instead of copying it.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 22, reprise of the opening melody combined with musette material. Analysis candidate at 188 seconds and the preceding reduction in level locate the broad return; this is not score-aligned timing.

transitions.title: Expansion before the quiet close
transitions.how: The closing passage expands the piano writing and builds to a last dynamic crest. Its aftermath is much quieter and increasingly spacious; written slowing eventually releases the triple pulse. The crescendo connects the returning material to the close rather than launching another full section of the dance.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 23, final expansion, reduction and slowing. Analysis candidates at 230 and 238 seconds; level rises from −19.7 at 235 to −8.3 at 250 before falling sharply.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
